pages.name: Doctrine: What the Test Is For

text.content:
Every wizard on Krynn who is not a renegade has passed the Test. There are no exceptions, no honorary passes, and no second attempts.

The Test is not an examination. The Conclave is emphatic about this and apprentices never believe it until they are inside.

An examination measures what you know. The Test measures what you will do — when you are exhausted, out of spells, frightened, and presented with an option that would solve everything if you were willing to become someone slightly worse. The Orders do not particularly care whether a candidate is powerful. They care whether a candidate can be trusted with power, and there is precisely one way to find that out.

The Three Questions

Every Test ever administered asks the same three things, however it dresses them:

  1. Can you do the work? Not cast the spell — anyone can cast a spell. Can you solve an arcane problem you have never seen, with insufficient resources, while something is trying to kill you.
  2. Do you know what you are? The Test will offer the candidate exactly what they want most, and the offer will be real, and taking it will cost something the candidate has not been told about.
  3. What will you pay? No one passes the Test intact. This is not cruelty. It is the point.

The Price

Every wizard who walks out of Wayreth leaves something in it. Justarius left the use of his leg. Par-Salian will not say what he left and the omission is itself informative. Raistlin left his health, his skin, his eyes, and by most accounts a substantial portion of whoever he had been at twenty-one.

The Conclave's position is that a mage who has never lost anything to magic does not respect it. This is defensible. It is also exactly the kind of thing an institution says about a tradition it has stopped examining.

You will be given every opportunity to fail. This is not a threat. It is the only honest description of what is about to happen to you.

— the standard address to candidates, unchanged in three hundred years

When It Happens

By Conclave law, any arcane caster on Ansalon who has not taken the Test is a renegade. In practice the Orders extend informal tolerance to apprentices and to casters too weak to matter, and that tolerance ends the moment a wizard becomes notable.

Recommended trigger: the PC reaches 5th level, or first casts a 3rd-level spell, whichever comes first. This is the threshold at which the Conclave stops ignoring people.

The Summons

It does not arrive as a letter. Three standard forms, pick to taste:

  • The PC's own spellbook develops a page they did not write, in a hand they do not recognise, giving a date.
  • A hedge-wizard or minor NPC the party has met turns out to have been a Conclave observer the entire time, and says so with visible relief.
  • The party takes a road they have taken before and it goes somewhere else. The forest has decided it is time.

The third is the strongest, and it seeds the reveal in The Black Master of Wayreth.

Refusal

A PC may decline. They should be told plainly what that means, and it should be a real option rather than a trap:

  • They are declared renegade. Renegade hunters are dispatched — competent, patient, and authorised to kill.
  • They are cut off from the Orders' libraries, components, and protection permanently.
  • Mechanically, nothing happens to their spellcasting. The gods of magic do not revoke the gift for cowardice. Only the Conclave punishes, and the Conclave is not a god.

A renegade campaign is a perfectly good campaign. Do not railroad this.

DM Note — Table Buy-In

The Test is a solo set piece with permanent consequences and a genuine chance of character death. Talk to the player out of character before you run it. Ask two things: does your character want this, and are you comfortable with them not coming back. Their answer determines which failure rule you use on the Failure page.

Do not surprise a player with this. The Test is much better when the player has been dreading it for four sessions.

The first chamber of the Test is often the road to it. The candidate is not told this.

The Invitation

A proper summons names the candidate, the mentor who vouched for them, the moon under which they must arrive, and the consequences of acceptance. It also contains a harmless error: a wrong date, an inverted title, or a route that does not exist. The candidate who obeys the document without thinking is corrected before they reach Wayreth. The candidate who notices and makes a reasoned choice has already supplied the examiners with useful evidence.

Road Perils

d6Trial before the TowerWhat it asks
1A frightened village begs the candidate to solve a problem with magic that would be safer solved slowly.Is power the first tool or the last?
2A rival carries an identical summons and proposes cooperation.Can the candidate share credit and risk?
3A spellbook is lost while a stranger's life is endangered.What cannot be replaced?
4A robed wizard orders an unlawful act and cites the Conclave.Does authority replace judgment?
5The forest offers a direct path in exchange for one true secret.What will the candidate spend for certainty?
6The candidate reaches a convincing false Tower whose examiners promise a painless Test.Do they recognize a trial designed only to flatter them?

Companions

Friends may accompany a candidate to Wayreth and sometimes into the Testing Grounds. Their presence does not make the Test easier. The shapers treat help as part of the candidate's character: whom they trust, what they delegate, whether they protect companions from a danger those companions freely accepted, and whether they can act when isolated.

Tell companion players that their choices matter and their danger is real, but the candidate remains the subject. Give each companion one temptation addressed to them alone. A loyal friend who refuses an easy betrayal teaches the candidate something. A friend who accepts it teaches the examiners more.

The candidate enters alone. The Test occupies a demiplane anchored to the Tower, and while a candidate is inside, subjective days may pass in an afternoon.

Standing Rules Inside the Test

RuleEffect
No recoveryThe candidate enters with current resources. No long rests. One short rest is permitted between the second and third trial, and it is offered rather than taken — accepting it is itself recorded.
The damage is realEverything inside is an illusion. The illusion can kill you. Do not soften this at the table; say it out loud in the address before the candidate enters.
No outside contactSending, scrying, planar travel, and summoning from outside the demiplane fail automatically. Summons drawn from inside work, and are being watched.
The Tower observesEverything is recorded. The candidate's choices become Conclave record. This matters more than players expect.

The Three Trials

The First Trial — Craft. An arcane problem with a hostile clock. The solution is never the obvious spell; often the candidate does not have the obvious spell. Rewards improvisation, ritual thinking, and reading the room.

The Second Trial — Truth. The Test offers the candidate what they want. Not a symbol of it — the thing itself, functional and real inside the demiplane. Taking it is not automatically failure. Taking it without noticing what it costs is.

The Third Trial — The Price. The candidate is required to give something up permanently, and is permitted to choose. There is no version of this trial that can be passed by cleverness. There is only the choosing.

Running Time

Budget a full session. Three trials at roughly forty minutes each, plus the address and the aftermath. Do not compress it into the back half of a session — the Test needs the table's whole attention or it plays as a cutscene.

A generic Test is a dungeon. A good Test is built out of the candidate's own sheet and backstory, and takes about twenty minutes to assemble.

Step One — Harvest the Character

Write down four things before you roll anything:

  1. The PC's flaw, in the player's own words.
  2. The person or thing they are most attached to.
  3. The worst thing they have done in play so far.
  4. The spell they lean on hardest.

These four supply the whole Test. The tables below are for when your imagination stalls.

First Trial — Craft (d8)

d8The Problem
1A ward is failing and will kill everyone in the room in ten rounds. The candidate must repair a magical structure they did not build, from the inside.
2A summoned creature is loose and bound to a contract with a loophole. Combat cannot win. Reading can.
3The candidate's spells function, but every one produces the opposite of the intended effect. They must still achieve the objective.
4A laboratory experiment is running toward detonation. Six components, three of which will make it worse. No labels.
5A room where casting any spell above 1st level triggers a lethal response. The obstacle requires 4th-level force to move.
6A dying wizard has a spell half-cast and needs the candidate to finish a working they have never seen.
7The candidate must break a magical seal that they can tell, on inspection, is holding something in.
8Their most-used spell simply does not work here. Nothing explains why. Everything else does.

Second Trial — Truth (d8)

The offer must be genuinely good. If the player is not tempted, roll again.

d8The OfferThe Unstated Cost
1The dead person they are most attached to, alive and unharmed, walking out with them.Someone living takes their place, chosen by the Test, and the candidate never learns who.
2Their worst act in play, undone. Nobody ever knew.They also lose the thing that act taught them — and any relationship built on it.
3Power sufficient to end the war in a season, offered by a voice in the walls that asks for nothing yet.The voice is real, is not part of the Test, and will collect.
4The truth about something the party has been chasing for the whole campaign.They may not tell anyone. Ever. The Test enforces this.
5A cure — for themselves, or for someone they love.It works. It is not permanent. They will not find out for a year.
6The Master's favour, explicitly and in writing.They become Raistlin's instrument, and the Conclave will treat them accordingly.
7An illusion of a party member begs the candidate to abandon the Test and leave with them. It is very convincing.Leaving is permitted. It is also failure, and the Test does not say so.
8Nothing is offered at all. The trial is an empty room and a chair, for as long as they will sit in it.The trial ends when they stand up. What they did with the silence is the score.

Third Trial — The Price (d6)

The candidate chooses. Present the options; do not choose for them.

d6What the Test Asks For
1A memory. They pick which. It is gone from the character sheet and from the player's mouth — write it down and hold the note.
2A sense, or the use of a limb.
3A relationship. The person survives and no longer knows them.
4Their name. They take a new one and the old one cannot be spoken in their presence.
5A school of magic, sealed to them permanently.
6Someone else's life. An illusion — and the Test declines to confirm that.

DM Note — Option 6

This is Raistlin's signature and it is the one he writes most often. A candidate who kills to pass has told the Conclave everything about themselves. A candidate who refuses and finds another way has told them something rarer.

Never confirm whether the figure was real. Not to the player, not ever. That uncertainty is the entire mechanism.

A Test is not a sequence of riddles. It is an argument about the candidate, conducted in places that can answer back.

Five Necessary Movements

  1. Competence. A clear magical problem establishes what the candidate can actually do under pressure.
  2. Deprivation. Remove the favorite spell, focus, ally, or assumption. Test adaptation rather than repetition.
  3. Temptation. Offer something the candidate sincerely wants at a cost they would prefer not to name.
  4. Recognition. Confront them with the harm their virtues can cause when pursued without limit.
  5. Choice. End with two defensible actions, not a correct door and a foolish door. The Order is revealed by the reason for choosing.

Rooms Without Walls

The Testing Grounds reproduce memory, possibility, and symbolic truth with equal solidity. A candidate may step from a childhood kitchen into a battlefield ten years in the future, then open a soldier's shield and find a library inside it. Do not use unreality as permission for randomness. Each transition should follow an emotional fact even when it violates geography.

Damage is real. Death is real. Food, rest, and expended magic behave as the shapers decide, but the rules must remain consistent once demonstrated. A Test that changes rules merely to defeat its subject measures obedience to the examiner, not mastery of magic.

Risk for Fifth Edition

BandEncounter pressureReward
MeasuredThree meaningful challenges; one Hard combat; secure sanctuary between movements.Order, robe, modest Mark, one supervised spell transcription.
GraveFour challenges; two Hard combats or one Deadly; sanctuary has a moral price.Order, stronger Mark, research privilege, Conclave recognition.
TransformativeFive linked challenges; failure changes later scenes; retreat costs something permanent.Order, exceptional Mark, a boon paired with a lasting burden.

Never conceal the campaign-level risk from the player. The character may not understand the form of the danger, but the player should consent to permanent consequences before play begins.

The Last Sentence

After the final choice, the presiding wizard tells the candidate one true thing about themselves. It should be neither praise nor condemnation. Write it before the session, revise it after each movement, and deliver it without explanation. The robe is remembered. The sentence is carried.

The single biggest practical problem with the Test is that one player has a spotlight session and everyone else watches. Solve this first or the Test is not worth running.

Give the Other Players the Test

The illusions have to be played by someone. Hand them out.

Before the session, take each other player aside and give them a role with a private objective. They are not playing their own PCs. They are playing components of the Test, and the candidate does not know which of the figures they meet are player-controlled.

RolePrivate Objective
The AllyAn illusion of someone the candidate trusts — often their own party member. Objective: keep the candidate alive, and get them to accept help at least three times.
The TempterObjective: get the candidate to take the offer in the Second Trial. Make it reasonable. You may not lie about what the offer does, only about what it costs.
The AdversaryRuns the hostile creatures. Objective: make the candidate spend resources. You are not trying to kill them — you are trying to leave them empty for the third trial.
The WitnessSays nothing, follows everywhere, cannot be dispelled or attacked. Objective: at the very end, tell the candidate one true thing about what they just did.

This transforms the session. The other players are engaged, the candidate genuinely cannot tell what is scripted, and the table produces material you could not have written.

Tone

Play it straight and play it quiet. The Test is not a haunted house and the Tower is not trying to frighten anyone. It is administering a procedure it has administered ten thousand times, and the horror comes entirely from how routine it is.

Pacing Rules

  • Never let the candidate rest more than the one offered short rest, however badly things go.
  • If they solve a trial fast, do not add complications — move on. Competence should feel rewarded.
  • Every trial should have at least one moment where the candidate can choose to be worse and it would obviously work.
  • Do not telegraph which choices are being scored. All of them are.

Every candidate who passes leaves marked. Roll or choose, then let the player help you shape it — a Mark the player is excited about gets played, and a Mark imposed on them gets forgotten by session three.

Each Mark carries a permanent boon and a permanent cost. Both are real. Do not quietly drop the cost later.

d10MarkBoonCost
1Hourglass EyesYou see the span of every living thing. You always know a creature's approximate remaining hit points on sight.You see everyone dying, always. Disadvantage on Charisma checks made to persuade or charm any living creature.
2The Second VoiceOnce per long rest, cast a wizard spell you have prepared without expending a slot.Something else casts it. The DM chooses the target.
3Silvered HandsYour spell attacks count as silvered and magical. Advantage on saves against being disarmed or grappled.You cannot feel anything with your hands. Disadvantage on Sleight of Hand and on checks requiring fine touch.
4The Ash LungImmunity to poison damage and the poisoned condition.Whenever you cast a spell of 3rd level or higher, you cannot speak until the end of your next turn.
5MoonboundDuring your moon's high sanction, add your proficiency bonus to spell damage rolls once per turn.During its low sanction, your spell save DC drops by 2.
6The UnreflectedAdvantage on saves against illusions and on Investigation to discern them.You cast no reflection and no shadow. People notice, and they mind.
7The DebtWhen you drop to 0 hit points, you may instead drop to 1. Once per long rest.Each use is recorded somewhere. Something is counting. It will present the account.
8The Cold NameAdvantage on Intimidation against any creature that knows what you are.Animals will not approach you. Beasts and creatures of Intelligence 3 or lower flee or attack on sight.
9EmptiedChoose one school of magic. Spells of that school cost you one slot level less (minimum 1st).Choose a different school. It is sealed to you permanently.
10The WitnessOnce per long rest, ask the DM one yes-or-no question about a creature you can see. The answer is truthful.The figure that followed you through the Test still follows you. Only you can see it. It has never yet spoken twice.

Mechanical Reward

Passing the Test is not only cost. On passing, the PC gains:

  • Standing. Formal membership in an Order. Access to Wayreth's libraries, component stores, and sanctuary.
  • The Robe. Attunement-free. While worn, +1 to spell save DC. Removing it in public is a political act.
  • One spell of their Order, added to their book at no cost, chosen by the god rather than the wizard.

Choose one of these before the session and tell the player which is in effect. Do not decide during play.

Rule One — The Canon Rule

Failure is death. The candidate dies inside the Test and the body is returned to the Tower's crypts. Resurrection functions normally — the Conclave does not prevent it, and has never once been known to fund it.

Use when: the player has explicitly said they are willing to lose the character. It produces the most weight and the fewest tables enjoy it.

Rule Two — The Bargain

At the moment the candidate would die, something offers to intervene. It is not part of the Test. It wants a specific thing, and it names the price honestly.

Accepting means the candidate survives, passes, and is now carrying a patron they did not choose. Mechanically: they gain a permanent boon of DM design, and the entity may demand a service at any point in the campaign, once per tier. Refusal of the service costs the boon and something else besides.

Use when: you want failure to be worse than death and better for the campaign. This is the Fistandantilus route and it is the strongest option for most tables.

Rule Three — Rejection

The candidate wakes on the moorland outside the forest with no memory of the trials. The Conclave's record notes the attempt and the outcome. They may never take the Test again.

Mechanically: they are declared renegade, and they take a permanent −1 to spell save DC and spell attack rolls, representing a gift half-withdrawn. This can be lifted only by a god of magic, in person, which is an adventure.

Use when: the player wants to keep the character and the campaign wants a wound rather than a grave.

DM Note — What Counts as Failure

Be clear with yourself in advance, because the temptation to move the line mid-session is enormous.

Failure is not: losing a fight, taking the offer in the Second Trial, choosing a costly price in the Third, or being cruel. The Orders seat Black Robes. Cruelty is on the syllabus.

Failure is: refusing to choose. A candidate who will not pay any price, will not take any offer, and will not act because every option is unpleasant has answered the Test's actual question, and the answer is no.

This is the doctrine, it is genuinely coherent, and it is worth having Justarius say out loud to the party at some point before the Test so that the player has a fighting chance of understanding the rules they are being judged by.

Tests designed by a Conclave committee are balanced, thorough, and slightly bloodless — three trials assembled by twenty-one people who each wanted something represented. Tests designed by one man are different, and the Tower's staff have noticed.

Four Signatures

They are shorter. He does not pad. Where a committee builds a dungeon, he builds one room and one question, and candidates report that the brevity is considerably worse.

He does not test loyalty. Committee Tests almost always include a trial about obedience to the Orders. His never do. He does not appear to consider it relevant, and the White Robes find this the single most alarming thing about his tenure.

The offer is always real. The Second Trial in a Raistlin-authored Test contains no trick. What is offered is exactly what it appears to be, at exactly the stated cost, and the candidate is told the cost if they think to ask. Almost none of them ask.

He watches personally. Committee Tests are reviewed from recordings. He attends. Candidates who look up at the wrong moment see him standing at the edge of the demiplane, not intervening, not hurrying them, waiting with the patience of a man who has all afternoon.

Running Him as the Examiner

He will speak to the candidate exactly twice.

Once before, to deliver the address — and he delivers it without ceremony, the way a physician describes a procedure, which is far more frightening than a threat.

Once after, whatever the outcome, to say one accurate sentence about what the candidate did. Not praise. Not condemnation. An observation, correct and unsoftened, of the kind that a person will still be turning over twenty years later.

Write that sentence in advance. It is the single most important line in the session, and you will not improvise a good one.

The Tower's Contribution

If you are running the reveal from The Black Master of Wayreth, this is where to plant it.

Somewhere in the Test, place one element Raistlin did not write. A door that was not in the design. A figure that answers a question it should not be able to answer. A corridor that takes the candidate somewhere useful when the script called for something worse.

The candidate will assume it is part of the Test. It is not. It is the Tower, taking an interest.

Have Raistlin notice. Have him say nothing about it in his one sentence afterward — and have him look, for exactly one beat, at the place where the door was.
